Migration direction⟦0⟧of dunes whose crests have the bed-instability orientation⟦1⟧: perpendicular to⟦2⟧, toward the side of the net sand flux across the crest (⟦3⟧;⟦4⟧).
° (compass bearing, clockwise from north, toward which sand moves)

Elongation direction⟦0⟧: the direction in which a dune grows in length without migrating, where the net sand flux across its crest is zero and the net flux along it is positive (⟦1⟧). It applies to dunes on beds with limited sand, typically growing from a fixed sand source. Where a wind regime allows several such directions, the atlas shows the most stable one.

Crest orientation⟦0⟧of the bed-instability mode: the axis (⟦#0⟧–⟦#1⟧°) of crests that receive the largest gross sand transport across them, including the speed-up of the wind over the crest (⟦1⟧;⟦2⟧). It is also the expected crest orientation of migrating dunes such as barchans. Dunes with this orientation migrate perpendicular to it, in direction⟦3⟧. As an axis it has no compass direction: e.g., ⟦#2⟧° and ⟦#3⟧° are the same line.

Direction⟦0⟧along crests of the bed-instability orientation⟦1⟧in which the net sand flux along the crest points, as a compass bearing. Where crests are oblique to the net transport, sand moves along them as well as across them;⟦2⟧shows which way along the crest it moves.
Limits span zero: symmetric log scale, linear close to zero
Log scale needs min > ⟦#0⟧, or min < ⟦#1⟧ < max (symmetric log)

Ratio of the growth rates in height of dunes in the elongation and bed-instability orientations,⟦0⟧, between ⟦#0⟧ and ⟦#1⟧. It assesses whether dunes elongating from a sand source on a starved bed are stable: in numerical simulations and in dunes around the Tibesti Massif, elongating linear dunes form where the ratio is above about ⟦#2⟧ and trains of barchans form below it (⟦1⟧;⟦2⟧). It does not take bed mobility or other boundary conditions into account.

Net along-crest over net across-crest sand flux for crests of the bed-instability orientation,⟦0⟧. Along-crest transport tends to keep crests straight, while across-crest transport, which drives migration, tends to make them sinuous (⟦1⟧), so higher values suggest straighter long-crested dunes on sand-covered beds. For dunes migrating on starved beds, the ratio measures the asymmetry of sand fluxes that makes dunes such as barchans asymmetric (⟦2⟧). In the sand-covered-bed examples of⟦3⟧it is about ⟦#0⟧ for transverse, ⟦#1⟧ for oblique and ⟦#2⟧ for longitudinal dunes. The ratio goes to infinity where its denominator (a net flux) goes to zero (shown clipped to ±⟦#3⟧).

Gross over net across-crest sand flux for crests of the bed-instability orientation,⟦0⟧, never below ⟦#0⟧: the balance between growth in height and migration. Values near ⟦#1⟧ mean that transport across the crest goes one way and the dunes mainly migrate; large values mean that it reverses, building the dunes up with little net migration, which may also favour straighter crests (⟦1⟧). In the sand-covered-bed examples of⟦2⟧it is about ⟦#2⟧ for transverse, ⟦#3⟧ for oblique and ⟦#4⟧ for longitudinal dunes. The ratio goes to infinity where its denominator (a net flux) goes to zero (shown clipped to ±⟦#5⟧).

Gross across-crest over net along-crest sand flux for dunes in the elongation orientation,⟦0⟧: the balance between growth in height and elongation. For dunes that elongate without migrating, it is the parameter expected to distinguish their shapes. Compared with⟦1⟧, it indicates whether elongation or migration is more likely to set dune shape and orientation on a starved bed: the dynamic with the larger ratio favours growth in height more and is expected to prevail (⟦2⟧). The ratio goes to infinity where its denominator (a net flux) goes to zero (shown clipped to ±⟦#0⟧).
Fraction of time flat-bed friction velocity is above threshold⟦0⟧.
Average above-threshold flat-bed friction velocity, normalised by threshold⟦0⟧.

Fraction of bed-instability-mode (⟦0⟧) crest flux that occurs while the flat-bed friction velocity exceeds threshold,⟦1⟧. ⟦#0⟧ where crest flux occurs only while the flat bed is below threshold; undefined where there is no crest flux.

Fraction of elongation-mode (⟦0⟧) crest flux that occurs while the flat-bed friction velocity exceeds threshold,⟦1⟧. ⟦#0⟧ where crest flux occurs only while the flat bed is below threshold; undefined where there is no crest flux.

Time-averaged flat-bed saturated sand flux,⟦0⟧over all speed and direction bins: the volume of packed sand per metre width that the wind could move per year over a flat bed fully covered by loose sand (⟦1⟧). Like the drift potential of⟦2⟧it measures the wind's capacity to transport sand, but it is a different quantity: Fryberger's⟦3⟧is in vector units, computed from ⟦#0⟧ m wind speeds in knots as⟦4⟧with a ⟦#1⟧-knot threshold, whereas this⟦5⟧is a physical flux computed from the friction velocity with the threshold set by the slider. The two cannot be converted into each other without the wind-speed distribution, and Fryberger's energy classes (below ⟦#2⟧, ⟦#3⟧–⟦#4⟧ and above ⟦#5⟧ vector units) do not apply to these values.

Magnitude of the time-averaged flat-bed flux vector,⟦0⟧: the net volume of packed sand per metre width per year after transport in opposing directions has cancelled. Same units as⟦1⟧;⟦2⟧≤⟦3⟧, with equality only when all transport is in one direction.

Direction of the time-averaged flat-bed flux vector,⟦0⟧, the direction sand moves, as a compass bearing (clockwise from north). Poorly defined where⟦1⟧is low, because transport in opposing directions nearly cancels.

Directional variability of sand flux: ratio of resultant to total drift potential,⟦0⟧(⟦#0⟧ = multidirectional, ⟦#1⟧ = unidirectional). Undefined where there is no sand flux (⟦1⟧).⟦2⟧classes: below ⟦#2⟧ low (complex or obtuse bimodal winds), ⟦#3⟧–⟦#4⟧ intermediate (obtuse to acute bimodal winds), above ⟦#5⟧ high (unimodal winds). Only transport above the threshold counts here, and the flux law differs from Fryberger's, so use the classes as a guide.

Divergence of the time-averaged saturated sand-flux vector (magnitude⟦0⟧, direction⟦1⟧) on the sphere, following⟦2⟧, Methods⟦3⟧:⟦4⟧with⟦5⟧,⟦6⟧. By conservation of sand mass, negative values (flux convergence) imply deposition and positive values (flux divergence) erosion. The values assume a saturated flux and an unlimited supply of loose sand, so on rock, crusted or vegetated surfaces actual erosion is limited by the sand available. No data at coasts (a neighbouring cell has no wind data) and on the ±⟦#0⟧° rows.

Global Aridity Index v3.1 (⟦#0⟧–⟦#1⟧): mean annual precipitation divided by reference evapotranspiration, native ⟦#2⟧″ (~⟦#3⟧ km) grid.⟦0⟧classes: < ⟦#4⟧ hyper-arid, ⟦#5⟧–⟦#6⟧ arid, ⟦#7⟧–⟦#8⟧ semi-arid, ⟦#9⟧–⟦#10⟧ dry sub-humid, > ⟦#11⟧ humid. Values of ⟦#12⟧ mean⟦1⟧≥ ⟦#13⟧ (source saturation). Ocean, Antarctica (south of ⟦#14⟧° S) and polar ice with zero⟦2⟧have no data.

Earth and Mars: what can be compared

Both atlases compute the same quantities with the methods outlined in⟦0⟧: the time-averaged saturated sand flux over a flat bed fully covered by loose sand (⟦1⟧), its resultant (⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧,⟦4⟧), crest fluxes, dune-orientation modes and flux divergence. Both report fluxes as volumes of packed sand (packing fraction ⟦#0⟧, pore space included) per metre width per Earth year of ⟦#1⟧ days (m²/yr), and both show wind roses as the direction the wind blows from and sand roses as the direction sand moves toward. They differ in four ways.

Control: on Earth the slider sets one threshold friction velocity⟦0⟧for the whole record (default ⟦#0⟧ m/s); on Mars it sets the median grain diameter d (default ⟦#1⟧ µm), and the threshold is computed for each time step of the wind record from d and that step's air density and temperature.

Transport law and wind profile: Earth uses the transport law of⟦0⟧, with⟦1⟧from the ⟦#0⟧ m wind and a roughness length of ⟦#1⟧ mm; Mars uses the transport law of⟦2⟧, with⟦3⟧from the wind at the lowest level of the wind dataset (its height above the surface differs between datasets) and a smooth-wall profile without a roughness length.

Winds and grid: Earth uses decades of hourly reanalysis winds (e.g.,⟦0⟧, ⟦#0⟧° grid, ⟦#1⟧–⟦#2⟧); Mars uses one Mars year (⟦#3⟧ sols, about ⟦#4⟧ Earth years) of winds from a climate-model simulation or a reanalysis (e.g.,⟦1⟧, ⟦#5⟧° grid), so one Mars cell can span several dune fields and year-to-year variability is not sampled.
Downloads: Earth cells provide a wind histogram and the fields against threshold (⟦0⟧,⟦1⟧); Mars cells provide the wind and air series and the fields against grain diameter (⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧).

⟦0⟧values on the two planets can therefore be compared in order of magnitude, not as precise numbers.⟦1⟧,⟦2⟧and the mode directions compare more directly, but each depends on the threshold or grain-diameter setting.

The atlas reads public⟦0⟧(v3) stores on data.geomorphlab.org, which anyone can read, e.g. with Python.
